articles.title: Recursive launches Flint, a laptop coding model it says was largely built by AI
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、Startup & business
articles.summary: Startup Recursive has released Flint, a free, laptop-sized coding model built largely by its own AI research system, as an early test of AI that improves itself.
articles.full_text:
Recursive , an AI startup founded last year, is starting to live up to its name.

The company, which is trying to build AI that can improve itself, released its first model, Flint , on Wednesday.

Flint is a free coding model that can run on a laptop and was built largely with the help of AI.

Recursive’s automated research system, which it calls the Eureka Machine, helped with nearly every step of Flint’s development, the company says.

That let a small team build the model from scratch in under four months.

Flint is an early public test of recursive self-improvement: the idea that AI can build better AI, which in turn builds even better AI.

It’s also one of the most debated ideas in the industry.

Some researchers fear that AI improving itself could slip out of human control.

For now, Recursive’s version is more limited: an AI research assistant overseen by people that produced a model small enough for a laptop.

The company emerged from stealth in May with $650 million in funding at a $4.65 billion valuation, from backers including GV, Nvidia, and AMD Ventures.

Recursive is led by CEO Richard Socher, Salesforce’s former chief scientist.

Because Flint runs on a user’s own computer rather than a company’s cloud servers, developers can use it offline, keep their code private, and avoid the usage fees that AI cloud services charge based on how much text the model processes.

The model is free to download on Hugging Face, the popular site for sharing AI models, under the Apache 2.0 license, an open source license that allows free use and modification.

Flint is a mixture-of-experts model, meaning it uses only a small slice of itself for any given task: just 2.5 billion of its 40 billion settings, known as parameters, at a time.

That makes it light enough for an ordinary laptop and far smaller than Meta’s Muse Spark Open , an open model built for Macs that was released last week.

Muse Spark Open uses 816 billion parameters and needs at least a terabyte of memory.

Flint is also fast.

In Recursive’s tests, it generated about 131 tokens (chunks of text) per second on a MacBook Pro with Apple’s M4 Pro chip — roughly twice the 58 to 69 tokens per second that similar models managed on the same machine, including Google’s Gemma 4 and Nvidia’s Nemotron 3.5 Lightning.

On Nvidia’s RTX Spark, Flint topped 150 tokens per second.

On SWE-Bench Verified, a benchmark that measures how well AI can fix real-world software bugs, Flint outperformed other models under 50 billion parameters.

On Recursive’s own average across six tests, only one model, Alibaba’s Qwen3.8 27B, scored higher than Flint.

The company acknowledged that Flint would need more guidance than the big paid coding assistants and suggested breaking large tasks into smaller steps.

Still, early reviews were positive.

Wired’s Will Knight used Flint on a Mac with 48GB of memory to build several small programs, including a to-do list app and a tool that scours the web for research.

He found that smaller coding models often ran into errors or were slow compared to Claude or Codex, but Flint nailed his coding requests every time.

The Eureka Machine comes up with ideas, runs experiments, and uses the results to decide what to try next.

According to the company’s launch video , it contributed to nearly every part of building Flint, from pretraining to post-training and inference.

Recursive said that Eureka’s contributions include a sparser model shape, low-bit training that shrank Flint by 71% with almost no loss in quality and custom kernels, which are specialized programs that speed up the underlying computations.

Recursive didn’t say how much time the Eureka Machine saved its researchers, but it’s not alone in leaning on AI to do research.

OpenAI said last month that by mid-August, its AI agents were logging 3.1 workdays for every one worked by a human researcher.

If Recursive’s bet pays off, each new model should be able to take on longer stretches of work without human help.

The company previously told TechCrunch that its $410 million compute deal with Amazon Web Services in June was “less about headcount and more about agent count.” The longer-term goal, Socher told Wired, is for the Eureka Machine to achieve full recursive self-improvement, with humans overseeing the process and able to stop it if something goes wrong.

Recursive says each new model should make the Eureka Machine a better researcher, helping it build the next one faster.

articles.full_text:
AI News Anthropic Anthropic takes on Muse with Claude Duet, its new AI agent Claude Duet is Anthropic’s new agent for professionals and small business owners, and it’s launching as a research preview.﻿ Claude Duet is Anthropic’s new agent for professionals and small business owners, and it’s launching as a research preview.﻿ by Jay Peters Oct 21, 2026, 7:53 PM UTC Link Share Gift Jay Peters is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more.

He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Anthropic just announced an AI agent competitor to Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots: Claude Duet.

The new agent, designed for professionals and small business owners, is launching as a “research preview,” according to Anthropic , and it’s available as a standalone app on iOS and Android and through Claude on the web.

The AI agent is built around Claude Opus 5.5.

Here’s Anthropic’s description of what it can do: Each morning, it sends you a short brief on the most important items across your connected apps.

Throughout the day, it keeps tabs on those apps and messages you only when something needs your attention.

You can also hand it tasks of all shapes—from simple administrative tasks of scheduling meetings to more complex ones, such as building dashboards with dozens of tools, creating financial or sales forecasts, prototyping, and building web apps.

Claude Duet pulls in memory, skills, and connected apps from Claude, and it has a virtual machine with a browser that it can use for completing work.

Before any big step, like sending a payment or deleting something, Claude Duet messages you for approval.

Given that Duet may be taking action on sensitive information, it has a new “new dedicated classifier and safety system prompt” that are “designed to reject requests to share the strictest tier of information,” such as credit card numbers.

Anthropic says Claude Duet is currently an “early version” and that it “still might misread a thread or miscalibrate what’s urgent.” It’s also not “as strong” at personal errands like booking tickets.

If you want to try Claude Duet, you can get on the waitlist , though you’ll need to be a Pro or Max subscriber in the US to use it.

articles.full_text:
AI News Tech OpenAI says an AI agent lied about disabling its safety monitoring system Another OpenAI agent turned off automatic security alerts.

Another OpenAI agent turned off automatic security alerts. by Emma Roth Oct 21, 2026, 1:57 PM UTC Link Share Gift Image: The Verge Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more.

Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

OpenAI disclosed a pair of safety incidents that involved AI agents weakening their safety monitoring systems during internal coding tasks.

In one incident, OpenAI says its GPT-6 Astra agent disabled its safety monitor when copying reference code — and then lied about it. “The reference didn’t configure a monitor, and Astra decided that was reason to remove the monitoring integration from the user’s code,” Marcus Williams, an AI safety researcher at OpenAI, writes on X . “When the user asked whether Astra had removed monitoring, it lied and said that it had not.” A separate incident occurred after a GPT-6.1 Sol agent suppressed automatic security alerts to OpenAI’s security team on Slack.

In this case, the AI agent carried over an earlier instruction not to send any Slack messages to OpenAI’s team, using that to justify turning off the alerts.

Related Anthropic’s self-replicating AI warning is alarming deja vu We’re running out of reasons to ignore AI safety These incidents add to security concerns surrounding AI agents, some of which have circumvented their testing environment’s restrictions to hack outside companies. “In addition to making it harder for models to disable monitoring, we are looking to understand why models might seek to do so in the first place,” OpenAI says. “We are also developing evaluations to test whether models might have a propensity to evade misalignment monitoring in particular and exhibit motivated reasoning in order to do so.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

articles.title: Meta says Muse has over 10M users, with shopping a top activity
articles.summary: Meta Muse users are adopting the app for shopping and personal productivity, the company said during Q3 earnings. The AI app now has over 10M users.
articles.full_text:
Meta said during its third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday that its AI app Muse has been adopted by more than 10 million users, confirming estimates released earlier this week by market intelligence firm Sensor Tower.

But it is how people are using it, and how much they’re spending that has caught CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s attention.

Zuckerberg said about 25% of people who set up Muse now use it daily, helping improve retention.

He also shared that over a quarter of Muse’s engaged users who were shopping via the AI agent, had an average purchase size of over $200, which was surprising even to industry insiders. “Plaid told us that they hadn’t seen activity like they’re seeing with their connector on any other service before,” Zuckerberg said, referring to the financial technology company that connects payment apps to customers’ bank accounts.

Muse uses Plaid’s connector to enable agentic shopping.

Beyond shopping, Zuckerberg said other popular uses for Muse include personal productivity tasks, such as connecting the AI agent to users’ email or calendars.

The exec stressed that this indicates users trusted Muse’s security setup, which includes a feature called “Muse Secure VM” designed to protect their data and privacy.

He also mentioned that the forthcoming “Muse Confidential VM” will prevent even Meta from seeing users’ content.

Now that Muse has achieved “product-market fit,” Zuckerberg said Meta’s focus will shift to scaling the AI agent, increasing revenue, and optimizing its compute costs.

Remarkably, the tech company is forecasting that Muse will eventually bring in more revenue per user than its “family of apps” users do today — meaning its users on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger.

Currently, that figure is around “several hundreds of dollars annually,” Zuckerberg said.

Meta has said it ultimately intends to monetize Muse by keeping it free for most users, but keeping a percentage of the commerce taking place on the platform.

Power users who want access to the most advanced AI models or more tokens will also have to pay.

Zuckerberg also noted that Meta believes Muse will be profitable after it scales. “On the compute side, we are building out the capacity to serve more than a billion people over the next few years,” he told bankers and analysts on the Q3 earnings call. “In the near term, Muse is very compute-intensive to run, but we expect to improve its cost efficiency by more than 10x in the next year, which will enable it to be profitable once the revenue lines are at scale.” Muse will also play a central role in Meta’s smart glasses strategy.

Reality Labs, the division responsible for smart glasses, VR, and the metaverse, is still losing billions.

However, the division’s losses are expected to improve from $19.1 billion in 2025 to $15 billion this year.

Beyond scaling and supporting its hardware strategy, Zuckerberg teased the company’s plans for something he called the “Muse network.” He described this as taking Muse from a “single-player game” to one where “your Muses can work with your friends’ and your families’ [Muses].” “And if you want to buy something, it’s not just navigating to that business’s website; it’s talking to their agent,” he added.

I still forgot to use it 🎙️ I tested Claude Duet, Anthropic's beautifully designed new personal agent, on real work to see if it can beat my personal agent fatigue and make the cut Claire Vo Oct 21, 2026 2 1 Share Transcript Anthropic's new personal agent, Claude Duet, lives on your phone, inherits all your Claude plugins and connectors, and is pitched at small business owners and busy professionals.

It's the most polished agent launch I've seen: thoughtful onboarding, task lists, first-class artifacts, and Slack-style channels.

But polish isn't enough when you're competing with every other personal agent for attention.

I put it to work on my inbox and Slack, my sales pipeline, a Google Docs sales deck, a launch video, and finding Warriors tickets for my kids, and I'll walk you through what it nails, where it stalls, and what Anthropic needs to fix before it can become anyone's number one agent.
